title: Electrical Appliances and Circuits
seo_title: Year 4 Science: Electrical Appliances and Circuits Worksheets (Will the Bulb Light?)
standard_text: Identify common appliances that run on electricity. Construct a simple series electrical circuit, identifying and naming its basic parts, including cells, wires, bulbs, switches and buzzers. Identify whether or not a lamp will light in a simple series circuit, based on whether or not the lamp is part of a complete loop with a battery. Recognise that a switch opens and closes a circuit and associate this with whether or not a lamp lights in a simple series circuit.
meta_desc: Free Year 4 science worksheets on electricity: mains and battery appliances, electrical safety, the parts of a circuit, switches, and whether a bulb will light. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: A complete loop makes a bulb light.
key_sub: Cells push electricity round wires; a switch opens or closes the loop.
body_html:
How to think about it

Appliances need electricity, from the mains or from batteries.

  • Mains electricity is powerful and dangerous; batteries (cells) are safe for experiments.
  • A simple circuit needs a cell and a complete loop of wires through a bulb, buzzer or motor.
  • A switch opens a gap (off) or closes it (on). Any gap stops the electricity.
Example

A bulb joined to a cell by one wire. Light?

The loop is not complete

Answer: No

Example

Kettle: mains or battery?

Big, powerful appliance

Answer: mains

Common mistakes

  • Thinking a bulb lights with one wire.
  • Thinking a switch makes a bulb brighter.
  • Touching plugs or switches with wet hands.

faq.q: What makes a bulb light up?
faq.a: A cell joined in a complete loop of wires through the bulb, with no gaps. Electricity can then flow all the way round.
It opens or closes a gap in the circuit. When it is closed (on), electricity flows; when it is open (off), it stops.

faq.q: What is the difference between mains and battery power?
faq.a: Mains electricity comes from power stations through plug sockets and is dangerous. Batteries (cells) store a small amount of electricity and are safe for school experiments.
